title: Azure Monitor: Activity Log, Metrics, and KQL
intro: Azure's observability has three parts. The Activity Log records who changed what (like AWS CloudTrail). Metrics are numbers over time. Log Analytics stores logs you query with KQL (Kusto Query Language), a pipe-based query language used across Azure, Sentinel, and Defender. KQL is worth learning properly.

steps.prompt: Show the last hour of changes in rg-web-prod from the Activity Log.
expected_commands: az monitor activity-log list --resource-group rg-web-prod --offset 1h --output table
az monitor activity-log list -g rg-web-prod --offset 1h -o table
steps.fake_output:
Caller              OperationName                                   Status     EventTimestamp
------------------  ----------------------------------------------  ---------  --------------------
bob@contoso.com     Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/write   Succeeded  2026-09-28T09:41:07Z
pipeline-sp         Microsoft.Web/sites/write                       Succeeded  2026-09-28T09:12:55Z
steps.explanation: bob changed an NSG at 09:41; a pipeline deployed the web app at 09:12.
steps.why: 'What changed just before it broke?' comes first in every investigation. The Activity Log keeps 90 days; export it to Log Analytics for longer retention and for joining with other logs.

steps.prompt: Get vm-web-01's CPU at 5-minute intervals. Its resource id is /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444/resourceGroups/rg-web-prod/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/vm-web-01.
expected_commands: az monitor metrics list --resource /subscriptions/33333333-dddd-4eee-8fff-444444444444/resourceGroups/rg-web-prod/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/vm-web-01 --metric "Percentage CPU" --interval PT5M
steps.explanation: CPU dropped from about 24% to 3% right after 09:41: traffic stopped arriving.
steps.why: Intervals use ISO 8601 durations (PT5M = 5 minutes). A sudden drop, not a spike, lines up with bob's NSG change at 09:41 and points straight at it.

steps.prompt: Query Log Analytics workspace 8b2c4d6e-1f3a-4b5c-9d7e-0a1b2c3d4e5f with KQL: count failed requests (resultCode 5xx) per 5 minutes from AppRequests over the last hour.
expected_commands: az monitor log-analytics query --workspace 8b2c4d6e-1f3a-4b5c-9d7e-0a1b2c3d4e5f --analytics-query "AppRequests | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) and ResultCode startswith '5' | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)"

az monitor log-analytics query -w 8b2c4d6e-1f3a-4b5c-9d7e-0a1b2c3d4e5f --analytics-query "AppRequests | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) and ResultCode startswith '5' | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)"
steps.fake_output:
TimeGenerated         count_
2026-09-28T09:35:00Z  0
2026-09-28T09:40:00Z  1
2026-09-28T09:45:00Z  0
(the few requests that arrive still succeed; the rest never reach the app)
steps.explanation: No wave of errors. Requests aren't failing in the app, they're not getting there.
steps.why: KQL reads left to right like a shell pipeline: table | where | summarize | render. 'summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)' is the pattern you'll use most. Here the lack of errors confirms the NSG theory: blocked traffic never shows up in application logs at all.

steps.prompt: List the alert rules that are configured, to see why nobody got paged.
expected_commands: az monitor metrics alert list --output table
az monitor metrics alert list -o table
steps.fake_output:
Name                 Severity  Enabled  Condition
-------------------  --------  -------  ----------------------------------
vm-web-cpu-high      2         True     avg Percentage CPU > 85
appgw-5xx-high       1         True     total ResponseStatus 5xx > 50
steps.explanation: Alerts exist for high CPU and many 5xx errors, but nothing fires when traffic simply stops.
steps.why: This is a classic monitoring gap: every alert watches for too much of something, and none watches for too little. Add a 'requests per minute below normal' alert, or better, an external availability test that probes the site from outside Azure.
